role: Mathematician, computing pioneer
title: Computing Machinery and Intelligence
summary: Proposed the 'imitation game' (Turing test) as an operational replacement for 'Can machines think?' and answered nine objections to machine intelligence.
quote: I believe that in about fifty years' time it will be possible to programme computers, with a storage capacity of about 10^9, to make them play the imitation game so well that an average interrogator will not have more than 70 per cent chance of making the right identification after five minutes of questioning.

prediction.text: Computers would play the imitation game well enough to fool an average interrogator 30% of the time after five minutes

role: Mathematician, computing pioneer
title: Intelligent Machinery, A Heretical Theory (lecture)
summary: In a 1951 lecture (published 1996 in Philosophia Mathematica), Turing argued thinking machines would soon outstrip humans and foresaw them taking control, the earliest statement of AI takeover by a computing founder.
quote: At some stage therefore we should have to expect the machines to take control, in the way that is mentioned in Samuel Butler's Erewhon.

prediction.text: Machines would eventually outstrip human powers and take control

role: Mathematician, founder of cybernetics
title: Some Moral and Technical Consequences of Automation (Science, 6 May 1960)
summary: Using Arthur Samuel's self-improving checkers program as his example, Wiener warned that learning machines can develop strategies faster than humans can understand or stop them, an early statement of what is now called the alignment problem.
quote: If we use, to achieve our purposes, a mechanical agency with whose operation we cannot efficiently interfere once we have started it ... then we had better be quite sure that the purpose put into the machine is the purpose which we really desire and not merely a colorful imitation of it.

role: Statistician, former Bletchley Park codebreaker with Turing
title: Speculations Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine
summary: Defined the 'ultraintelligent machine' and argued it could design ever-better machines, setting off an 'intelligence explosion', with control as the key condition.
quote: Thus the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control.

prediction.text: An ultraintelligent machine would set off an 'intelligence explosion' (in the paper Good also judged it more likely than not to be built within the 20th century; that line was not checked against the original text here)

role: AI pioneer, cognitive psychologist, economist (later Nobel laureate)
title: The Shape of Automation for Men and Management
summary: One of the famous early AI optimist forecasts. Simon predicted that machines would soon match human workers at any task, a timeline that slipped badly.
quote: machines will be capable, within twenty years, of doing any work a man can do.

prediction.text: Machines able to do any work a man can do

role: AI pioneer, co-founder of MIT AI Lab
title: Interview in Life magazine (1970), and 'Will Robots Inherit the Earth?' (Scientific American, 1994)
summary: Minsky made some of the boldest early timelines (human-level AI within 3 to 8 years, 1970). In 1994 he reframed future machines as humanity's successors, adopting Moravec's idea of 'mind children'.
quote: In from three to eight years we will have a machine with the general intelligence of an average human being.

prediction.text: A machine with the general intelligence of an average human

person: Geoffrey Hinton (with David Rumelhart & Ronald Williams)
role: Cognitive psychologist turned neural-network researcher (BA in experimental psychology); brain-inspired, but not a neuroscientist
title: Learning representations by back-propagating errors (Nature 323)
summary: Popularized backpropagation for training multilayer 'neurone-like' networks, showing that hidden units learn useful internal features. This became the core training method of later deep learning. Hinton's 2007 Google Tech Talk 'The Next Generation of Neural Networks' marked the deep-belief-net revival.
quote: We describe a new learning procedure, back-propagation, for networks of neurone-like units.
video_note: 2007 Google Tech Talk found at youtube.com/watch?v=AyzOUbkUf3M, but oEmbed returned 'Unauthorized' (embedding disabled), so it was excluded

role: Roboticist, Carnegie Mellon
title: Mind Children: The Future of Robot and Human Intelligence
summary: Argued from compute trends that robots would reach human-level intelligence within decades and become humanity's 'mind children', a postbiological successor species.
quote: It is a world in which the human race has been swept away by the tide of cultural change, usurped by its own artificial progeny.

prediction.text: Human-equivalence in robots within about forty years (Harvard UP blurb); robots evolve into new artificial species starting around 2030 to 2040

role: Mathematician, computer scientist, science-fiction author
title: The Coming Technological Singularity: How to Survive in the Post-Human Era (NASA VISION-21 symposium)
summary: Popularized the 'Singularity': superhuman intelligence created through AI, networks, interfaces or biology would end the human era, and progress beyond that point cannot be predicted. Vinge asked whether it could be avoided or guided.
quote: Within thirty years, we will have the technological means to create superhuman intelligence. Shortly after, the human era will be ended.

prediction.text: Superhuman intelligence; 'I'll be surprised if this event occurs before 2005 or after 2030'

role: Inventor, futurist
title: The Age of Spiritual Machines
summary: Laid out decade-by-decade predictions (2009, 2019, 2029, 2099) driven by his 'law of accelerating returns'. Its quotation of the Unabomber manifesto prompted Bill Joy's alarm.

prediction.text: A machine will pass the Turing test

role: Co-founder and chief scientist, Sun Microsystems
title: Why the Future Doesn't Need Us (Wired, April 2000)
summary: A leading technologist warned that robotics, genetic engineering and nanotech, all self-replicating 21st-century technologies, could make humans an endangered species, and floated relinquishing some research.
quote: Our most powerful 21st-century technologies—robotics, genetic engineering, and nanotech—are threatening to make humans an endangered species.
quote_note: This line is the article's standfirst (subtitle) on Wired.com

role: AI researcher, co-founder of the Singularity Institute for Artificial Intelligence (SIAI, now MIRI), incorporated July 2000
title: Creating Friendly AI 1.0: The Analysis and Design of Benevolent Goal Architectures
summary: Book-length document coining 'Friendly AI': the goal system of a self-improving AI must be designed so the AI stays benevolent. Yudkowsky argued friendliness will not emerge by default.
quote: Beyond this lies another question—whether the creation of this mind will benefit the world; whether the AI will take actions that are benevolent or malevolent, safe or uncaring, helpful or hostile.

role: Philosopher, Oxford (founded the Future of Humanity Institute in 2005)
title: Existential Risks: Analyzing Human Extinction Scenarios and Related Hazards (Journal of Evolution and Technology)
summary: Defined 'existential risk' as its own category and listed badly programmed superintelligence among the main ones, which set the frame for later AI x-risk work.
quote: One where an adverse outcome would either annihilate Earth-originating intelligent life or permanently and drastically curtail its potential.
youtube_title: Nick Bostrom: Humanity's biggest problems aren't what you think they are
video_note: TEDGlobal 2005 talk ('A philosophical quest for our biggest problems')

role: Philosopher, Oxford
title: Ethical Issues in Advanced Artificial Intelligence
summary: Introduced the paperclip-maximizer thought experiment: a superintelligence may pursue an arbitrary goal and resist any change to it, so intelligence and final goals are independent.
quote: It also seems perfectly possible to have a superintelligence whose sole goal is something completely arbitrary, such as to manufacture as many paperclips as possible, and who would resist with all its might any attempt to alter this goal.

role: Palm/Treo inventor turned neuroscientist; founded Redwood Neuroscience Institute (2002) and Numenta (2005)
title: How brain science will change computing (TED 2003) / On Intelligence (book, 2004)
summary: Argued the neocortex is a memory-prediction system, not a fast processor, and that real intelligent machines must be built on brain principles. He was sceptical of a runaway 'intelligence explosion'.
quote: Intelligence is largely defined by experience and training, not just by brain size or algorithms.
quote_note: From IEEE Spectrum, June 2008, on whether the singularity will occur ('then it will never happen')

prediction.text: 2004 Wired interview: brain-based intelligent machines would be 'a really exciting and hot industry' within ten years, possibly in two or three

role: Inventor, futurist
title: The Singularity Is Near (book) and TED2005 'The accelerating power of technology'
summary: Extended his exponential-trends case: brain reverse-engineered by the 2020s, human-level AI by 2029, and a Singularity of human-machine merger by 2045.
quote: I set the date for the Singularity—representing a profound and disruptive transformation in human capability—as 2045.

prediction.text: Singularity (with human-level AI / Turing test by 2029)

role: Cognitive scientist, author of Gödel, Escher, Bach
title: Trying to Muse Rationally about the Singularity Scenario (Singularity Summit at Stanford)
summary: Organized the 2000 Stanford 'Spiritual Robots' symposium (Kurzweil, Moravec, Joy) and spoke at the first Singularity Summit. He took the scenario seriously but doubted it would come soon, while warning that humans might be eclipsed.
quote: I think life and intelligence are far more complex than the current singularitarians seem to believe, so I doubt it will happen in the next couple of centuries.

prediction.text: Singularity possible 'someday in the distant future', not within the next couple of centuries

role: Physicist and AI researcher, Self-Aware Systems
title: The Basic AI Drives (Proceedings of the First AGI Conference)
summary: Argued that almost any sufficiently advanced goal-seeking AI will develop instrumental drives such as self-improvement, self-protection, protecting its goals and acquiring resources, unless designed against them. This became the basis of 'instrumental convergence'.
quote: One might imagine that AI systems with harmless goals will be harmless. This paper instead shows that intelligent systems will need to be carefully designed to prevent them from behaving in harmful ways.
youtube_title: Steve Omohundro on the Nature of Self-Improving Artificial Intelligence

role: Neuroscientist, director of EPFL Blue Brain Project
title: A brain in a supercomputer (TEDGlobal 2009)
summary: Described Blue Brain's cell-by-cell simulation of the rat neocortical column and claimed that a detailed, functional simulation of the human brain was a decade away.
quote: It is not impossible to build a human brain and we can do it in 10 years ... And if we do succeed, we will send a hologram to TED to talk.

prediction.text: A detailed, functional artificial human brain built (simulated) within 10 years

youtube_title: A brain in a supercomputer | Henry Markram

role: Cognitive neuroscientist (UCL PhD, Gatsby Unit postdoc); co-founded DeepMind in 2010
title: Combining systems neuroscience and machine learning: a new approach to AGI (Singularity Summit 2010)
summary: Months before DeepMind's founding, Hassabis argued that AGI should be built by combining brain-inspired high-level architecture from systems neuroscience with machine-learning algorithms, rather than symbolic AI.
quote: By bringing these two fields together, we can have both a high level architecture for an artificial general intelligence, and working algorithms for implementing many of the required components.

role: AI researcher (PhD under Marcus Hutter; later neuroscience postdoc at UCL Gatsby Unit); co-founded DeepMind in 2010
title: Machine Super Intelligence (PhD thesis, 2008) and 'Goodbye 2011, hello 2012' (vetta.org blog)
summary: His thesis formalized universal machine intelligence and openly discussed superintelligence. On his blog he kept a public AGI forecast: log-normal with mode 2025 and mean 2028. He has held it since 2009 and reaffirmed it in 2023.
quote: I give it a log-normal distribution with a mean of 2028 and a mode of 2025, under the assumption that nothing crazy happens like a nuclear war.

prediction.text: Human-level AGI (mean 2028, mode 2025); an impressive proto-AGI within 8 years. In a June 2011 Q&A his 10/50/90% dates were 2018/2028/2050
